title: Special relativity
summary: Learn why the speed of light is constant, and meet time dilation, length contraction and E = mc².
cards.0.p: In classical physics, velocities add. A ball thrown at 20 m/s relative to a train moving at 30 m/s travels at 50 m/s relative to the ground. With light, measurements always give c.
cards.0.key: Classical velocity addition works at everyday speeds, but it fails for light.
cards.1.h: The ether and the Michelson–Morley experiment
cards.1.p: In the 19th century, light was thought to travel through a medium called the ether. In 1887 Michelson and Morley looked for a difference in the speed of light with direction. They found no difference, and the ether was never found.
cards.1.key: The Michelson–Morley experiment showed that the speed of light does not depend on direction. So there is no ether.
cards.2.p: In 1905 Einstein put forward two postulates. First, the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. Second, the speed of light in a vacuum is c ≈ 3·108 m/s for everyone.
cards.2.key: An inertial frame is one that moves at constant velocity. No experiment can tell which frame is really at rest. The speed of light does not add to other speeds.
cards.3.p: The time measured in the frame where the events happen at the same place is called proper time (Δt0). A moving observer measures a longer time: Δt = γ·Δt0. Here γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²).
cards.3.key: At 0.6c, γ = 1.25. While 4 years pass on the ship, 5 years pass as seen from Earth. Proper time is the shortest time.
cards.3.etk.soru: Change the speed of the ship. While the clock on the ship measures Δt<sub>0</sub>, what does the clock on Earth measure?
cards.4.h: The γ factor and everyday speeds
cards.4.p: γ is never less than 1. For a jet flying at 300 m/s, γ ≈ 1 + 5·10<sup>−13</sup>, a difference only an atomic clock can measure. As the speed gets close to c, γ grows quickly.
cards.4.key: At everyday speeds γ ≈ 1 and relativity turns into Newtonian physics.
cards.5.p: The length of an object measured in its own frame is called its proper length (L0). A moving observer measures it shorter: L = L0/γ. The contraction happens only along the direction of motion.
cards.5.key: At 0.6c, γ = 1.25: a 100 m ship is measured as 80 m. Perpendicular dimensions stay the same.
cards.6.h: Relativistic momentum and the c limit
cards.6.p: At high speeds momentum is p = γ·m·v. As v gets close to c, γ and the energy needed grow without limit. That is why no object with mass can reach c.
cards.6.key: Only massless particles such as the photon move at c.
cards.7.p: Even an object at rest has rest energy: E0 = m·c². A mass of 1 g corresponds to 9·1013 J of energy. The mass Δm lost in fission and fusion is released as an energy of Δm·c².
cards.7.key: Fission is the splitting of a nucleus, and fusion is the joining of nuclei. You will see binding energy and mass defect in the topic “The atomic nucleus and radioactivity”.
cards.7.once.soru: With E = m·c², how many joules is 1 g of mass? (c = 3·10⁸ m/s)
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: This value is for 1 kg. 1 g is one thousandth of it.
cards.8.p: The total energy of a moving object is E = γ·m·c², and its kinetic energy is Ek = (γ − 1)·m·c². At low speed this reduces to ½mv². Mass does not grow with speed; what grows is γ.
cards.8.svg#12: m does not change; γ grows
cards.8.key: The relativistic mass γ·m found in some books is really γ entering momentum and energy. Mass (m) is constant.
cards.8.once.soru: For an object moving at 0.6c, γ = 1.25. What fraction of m·c² is its kinetic energy?
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: That is the total energy. The rest energy must be subtracted.
cards.9.p: The clocks on GPS satellites fall behind by about 7 μs a day because of their speed. Because of the weaker gravity they run ahead by about 45 μs a day. Without this correction, the position error would grow by about 10 km a day.
cards.9.key: The satellites orbit at a height of ≈20 200 km at ≈3.9 km/s. GPS applies both the special (speed) and the general (gravity) relativity correction.
cards.9.once.soru: Is relativity taken into account so that the GPS in your phone works correctly?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: Clock differences of microseconds cause position errors of kilometers.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: The difference is small, but multiplied by the speed of light it reaches kilometers.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: The satellite clocks are corrected for every user.
cards.10.p:
• Everyone measures the speed of light as c, and there is no ether.
• Simultaneity is relative.
• Time dilates: Δt = γ·Δt0.
• Length contracts along the motion: L = L0/γ.
• An object with mass cannot reach c, and E0 = m·c².
• When v ≪ c, γ ≈ 1.
quiz.0.q: On a ship moving at 0.6c relative to Earth, 12 years pass by the ship's clock. How many years pass for an observer on Earth?
quiz.0.e: At 0.6c, γ = 1/√(1 − 0.36) = 1.25. The time on the ship is the proper time. So Δt = 1.25·12 = 15 years.
quiz.1.q: For two observers moving at constant velocity relative to each other, put each quantity in the right group.
quiz.1.ogeler.0.0: Speed of light in a vacuum
quiz.1.e: By Einstein's postulates, the laws of physics and the speed of light in a vacuum are the same for everyone. Simultaneity, time intervals and length along the direction of motion depend on the observer. Length perpendicular to the motion does not contract.
quiz.2.q: Match each concept with its example.
quiz.2.ciftler.0.1: A muon's lifetime is measured longer from the ground
quiz.2.ciftler.1.1: A fast ship is measured shorter from the ground
quiz.2.e: Because the muon moves fast, its lifetime is measured γ times longer from the ground. A fast ship is measured γ times shorter along its motion. By E<sub>0</sub> = m·c², 1 g of mass equals 9·10<sup>13</sup> J. Michelson and Morley did not see the expected shift.
quiz.3.q: Which is true for an astronaut on a ship moving very fast relative to Earth?
quiz.3.o.0: They notice their own clock running slow.
quiz.3.o.1: They see the things on the ship as contracted.
quiz.3.o.2: They can exceed c by running the engines long enough.
quiz.3.o.3: They see their own clock running normally.
quiz.3.e: The astronaut is at rest in their own frame, and everything there runs normally. Time dilation and length contraction show up in the measurements of an observer moving relative to the ship.
quiz.3.y.0: The astronaut sees their own clock running normally. It is the observer on Earth who measures the clock as slow.
quiz.3.y.1: For the astronaut, the ship and the things on it are at rest. Only the observer on Earth measures the contraction.
quiz.3.y.2: As an object with mass speeds up, the energy needed goes to infinity. So the object cannot reach the speed of light or exceed it.
A:ozet: Add velocities and measure the speed of light. Find the order of the lightning strikes, speed up the light clock and make γ equal 2. Bring the muon to the ground, shorten the ship and push against the c limit.
A:adimlar.0.metin: A ball thrown forward from the train moves at 20 m/s relative to the train. What is its speed for an observer on the ground? Speed up the train so that the ball moves at 50 m/s relative to the ground. Then press play.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: 30 + 20 = 50 m/s. This is how velocities add in classical physics, and it is correct at everyday speeds. So does the light from the train's headlight travel at c + v relative to the ground?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.ipucu: The ball's speed relative to the ground is the train's speed plus 20. The sum must be 50.
A:adimlar.1.baslik: The speed of light is c for everyone
A:adimlar.1.metin: A ship approaches Earth at 0.5c and turns on its headlight.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: At what speed does an observer on Earth measure the headlight's light?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: That is what classical velocity addition would say. But the rule fails for light, and measurements always give c.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Measurements always give c. So the speed of light does not add to the motion of the source. Einstein took this as a postulate (next card).
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Light does not leave the source slowed down. Both the ship and Earth measure c.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Lightning strikes the two ends of a moving train, A and B. The two flashes reach O, standing on the ground exactly in the middle, at the same time. O′, in the middle of the train, is moving toward B. Both flashes travel at c.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: What order of lightning strikes does O′ conclude?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: They struck at the same time
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: O′ sees the flashes at different moments and knows both traveled at c. So O′ cannot say the lightning struck at the same time.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: O′ is moving away from A. So the light from A reaches O′ later.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: O′ moves toward the light ahead and sees it first. Since both flashes travel at c, O′ concludes that B was struck first. Events that are simultaneous in one frame may not be simultaneous in another.
A:adimlar.3.baslik: The light clock and time dilation
A:adimlar.3.metin: The time a moving observer measures is Δt = γ·Δt₀, with γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). In the light clock on the ship, light travels straight between two mirrors. Seen from Earth it takes a slanted, longer path, but its speed is still c. 6 years pass on the ship. Set the speed so that 10 years pass on Earth.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: At 0.8c, γ = 1/√(1 − 0.64) = 5/3. Δt = γ·Δt0 = 5/3 · 6 = 10 years. The time on the ship, where the events happen at the same place, is the proper time. Proper time is the shortest time, and it is always measured longer from other frames.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.ipucu: γ must be 10 / 6 = 5/3. Since γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²), γ grows as you raise v/c.
A:adimlar.4.metin: γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). Set the speed so that the moving clock runs at half speed as seen from Earth, which means γ equals 2.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.ipucu: For γ = 2, √(1 − v²/c²) must be 1/2. Raise the speed a little above 0.8c.
A:adimlar.5.baslik: How do muons reach the ground?
A:adimlar.5.metin: Cosmic rays produce muons in the atmosphere. The mean lifetime of a muon at rest is 2.2 μs. At 0.995c a muon can travel only 660 m in that time. A muon was born 6.6 km above the ground.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: Can the muon reach the ground within its mean lifetime?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: At 0.995c, γ is about 10. Seen from the ground, the muon's lifetime is about 22 μs, and in that time it travels about 6.6 km. In the muon's own frame, the atmosphere is γ times thinner, about 660 m.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: 2.2 μs is the lifetime by the muon's own clock. Seen from the ground, a moving clock runs slow.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: Only if it goes faster than light
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The muon moves at 0.995c. No object with mass can reach c.
A:adimlar.6.metin: The ship's length measured in its own frame, its proper length, is 100 m. An observer on Earth measuring the moving ship finds it shorter: L = L0/γ. Set the speed so that the ship measures 60 m.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.tamam: At 0.8c, γ = 1/√(1 − 0.64) = 5/3 and L = 100 / (5/3) = 60 m. The ship's height stays 20 m. The astronaut on board always measures their own ship as 100 m.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.ipucu: Since 100 / 60 = 5/3, γ must be 5/3. Raise the speed little by little.
A:adimlar.7.metin: At high speeds momentum is p = γ·m·v. Give the ship energy step by step and compare Newton's prediction with reality.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.soru: If you keep the engines running without stopping, what happens to the ship's speed?
A:adimlar.7.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: It passes c after a while
A:adimlar.7.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: That is what Newtonian physics would say. But since γ grows without limit, the speed always stays below c.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: It approaches c but never reaches it
A:adimlar.7.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: As v gets close to c, γ grows without limit. The energy needed to speed up a little more also grows without limit.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: It reaches exactly c and stays there
A:adimlar.7.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Reaching c takes infinite energy. So for an object with mass, v < c always.
A:kapanis.0: Classical velocity addition works at everyday speeds, but it fails for light. Everyone measures the speed of light as c.
A:kapanis.2: Time dilation is found with Δt = γ·Δt₀, where γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²).
A:kapanis.3: Length contracts only along the direction of motion: L = L₀/γ.
A:kapanis.4: An object with mass cannot reach c. Rest energy is E₀ = m·c².
A:kapanis.5: When v ≪ c, γ ≈ 1 and relativity turns into Newtonian physics.
